multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.

## Overview

Original Game Boy Advance emulator built from scratch in Rust, targeting `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Implements all major GBA hardware subsystems: ARM7TDMI CPU (ARM + Thumb), memory bus, PPU, DMA, timers, interrupts, and audio (PSG + DirectSound FIFO).

# Handoff: GBA Emulator (agbrs)

## Overview

Original Game Boy Advance emulator built from scratch in Rust, targeting `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Implements all major GBA hardware subsystems: ARM7TDMI CPU (ARM + Thumb), memory bus, PPU, DMA, timers, interrupts, and audio (PSG + DirectSound FIFO).

## Approach

### Phase 1: Research & scaffold
Read through GBATEK and the ABI spec. Set up the Cargo project with correct `cdylib` crate type and the 10 required C-ABI exports. Got a blank wasm compiling first before writing any emulation logic.

### Phase 2: CPU + Memory (highest leverage)
Implemented the ARM7TDMI with all data processing, multiply, single/block transfer, and branch instructions for both ARM and Thumb modes. Built the memory bus with correct address mapping for all GBA regions (BIOS, EWRAM, IWRAM, IO, Palette, VRAM, OAM, ROM, SRAM). Loaded the provided BIOS stub at 0x00000000.

Key decisions:
- 3-stage pipeline model: PC always reads as current_instruction + 8 (ARM) or + 4 (Thumb)
- Wrapping arithmetic everywhere to satisfy the zero-panic policy
- Open-bus reads for unmapped regions instead of crashing
- 16-bit IO bus routing: `read_io8` delegates to `read_io16` and extracts the right byte

### Phase 3: PPU
Scanline-based renderer running at cycle 960 (end of HDRAW). Supports:
- Modes 0-2 (tiled backgrounds with regular and affine layers)
- Modes 3-5 (bitmap modes)
- OAM sprites (regular and affine, all sizes)
- Windowing (WIN0, WIN1, OBJ window)
- Alpha blending and brightness effects
- Priority-based layer compositing

### Phase 4: DMA, Timers, Audio
- 4 DMA channels with priority ordering and audio FIFO triggers
- 4 cascading timers with prescaler dividers
- PSG channels 1-4 (square waves, wave RAM, noise)
- DirectSound FIFO A and B at 32768 Hz stereo

### Phase 5: Debug & iterate
Used the grader and oracle tools to identify failing tests and fix specific issues:
- LDM/STM block transfer had wrong base address calculation for DA/DB modes
- Thumb Format 8 had swapped operands (LDSB vs LDRH)
- IO register reads needed 16-bit bus alignment
- DMA registers returned wrong open-bus values
- Register-specified shifts needed PC+12 for R15 reads

## Architecture

```
src/
├── lib.rs          # WASM ABI exports (10 C-ABI functions)
├── gba.rs          # Top-level Gba struct, frame loop
├── cpu/
│   ├── mod.rs      # Pipeline, mode switching, interrupt handling
│   ├── arm.rs      # ARM instruction decoder/executor
│   ├── thumb.rs    # Thumb instruction decoder/executor
│   ├── alu.rs      # ALU operations with flag computation
│   └── registers.rs # Banked register definitions
├── bus/
│   ├── mod.rs      # Memory map, read/write dispatch
│   ├── io.rs       # IO register bitfield constants
│   └── waitstates.rs # ROM waitstate configuration
├── ppu/
│   └── mod.rs      # Scanline renderer, all BG modes, sprites
├── dma/
│   └── mod.rs      # 4-channel DMA controller
├── timer/
│   └── mod.rs      # 4 cascading timers
└── apu/
    └── mod.rs      # PSG + DirectSound FIFO audio
```

Total: ~4,500 lines of Rust.

## 2026-11-07 pass: timing, audio and differential testing

This pass was done with Claude Code (model: Claude Opus 5.5) driven by the
repository owner. Goal: check the repo against the take-home requirements,
find why the score was low, and raise it with validated changes.

### Score (gba-eval grader, native build, reference = bundled Mesen2)

| Run | Overall | Replay (60%) | Procedural (20%) | Audio (20%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (`dist/` wasm at commit e549c6a) | 0.3789 | 0.4606 | 0.4261 | 0.0865 |
| Intermediate (v8: APU rewrite, access timing, frame/boot alignment) | 0.5655 | 0.5537 | 0.5861 | 0.5802 |
| v11 (+ lockstep-derived IRQ/DMA/prefetch rules, input latching) | 0.6775 | 0.7137 | 0.5861 | 0.6605 |
| **Final** (`dist/gba_emu.wasm`, sha256 b2705a31…) | **0.6900** | **0.7181** | **0.5861** | **0.7096** |

Per-testcase tables: `results/` (baseline, v8, final), produced by
`tools/scores.py`.

### What was wrong (root causes found)
1. **Timing model unused.** A waitstate table existed but no instruction
   was ever charged memory waitstates; every instruction cost a fixed 1-3
   cycles, so games ran several times too fast relative to the PPU.
2. **HALT never halted.** HALTCNT was stored but the CPU kept running.
3. **APU clocked for the Game Boy, not the GBA.** Square/wave/noise timers
   used GB multipliers (pitch 4x too high), the frame sequencer
   (length/envelope/sweep) did not exist, and timers advanced at most one
   step per call. tonc-snd1 audio went 0.10 → 1.00 after the rewrite.
4. **Branch detection bug.** `step()` decided "no branch" by comparing r15
   before/after; a BX to the next word or `b .` refills to the same r15,
   so an extra ARM word was fetched. chip-advance hung in its crt0 because
   of this (video 0.03 before).
5. **Frame boundary and boot alignment.** The reference ends frames at
   VBlank start and reports 6 boot frames (`emu_boot_frames`); we ended
   frames at line 0 and reported 0, so every replay was phase-shifted.
6. **Input applied one frame early.** The reference latches keys at the
   frame boundary; we applied them immediately (goodboy: 840 → 48
   differing frames of 900).
7. **Fixed 32768 Hz output.** Games selecting 65536 Hz via SOUNDBIAS get
   twice the samples from the reference; the grader compares streams
   sample-for-sample (piugba audio 0.06 → 0.70).
8. **Mosaic not implemented; darken rounding off by one** (chip-advance
   fades).
9. Many smaller hardware rules (VRAM mirror hole in bitmap modes, open
   bus = last prefetched opcode, BIOS read protection, ROM out-of-range
   reads, DMA masks/latch/ROM-increment, DISPSTAT byte writes clearing
   status bits, PPU lagging one scanline per call after long DMAs,
   write-only DMA registers reading 0, timer start/stop latency).

### Method
- Baseline first, then every change validated with the real grader
  (`tools/quick-grade.sh` on subsets, `tools/grade.sh` for full runs).
- **Instruction-level lockstep against the reference** (`tools/lockstep`):
  runs `reference/mesen.wasm` one instruction at a time beside our core and
  reports the first PC/cycle divergence with per-access logs. This turned
  timing work from guesswork into measurement; see `docs/TIMING_MODEL.md`
  for every rule and its evidence. goodboy-advance now runs 8M+
  instructions in exact PC lockstep.
- Regression tests for each fixed bug: `tests/regressions.rs`.

### Known limitations after this pass
See `docs/TIMING_MODEL.md` "Known gaps": PPU/CPU VRAM contention not
modelled, prefetch-buffer and DMA edge cases (±1 cycle), a few IRQ
boundaries, timer reload-while-running, multiply-long carry flag,
mgba-io-read (48/130), mgba-dma (1248/1256).

### What I'd do next
1. Model VRAM/palette/OAM contention from the PPU's fetch schedule (the
   tracer's `--vram-stats` gives the target histogram). This is now the
   largest source of drift in mode-0 games.
2. Fit the remaining IRQ sampling rule with `--irq-report` data across
   all games.
3. Finish prefetch/DMA edge cases with `--branch-stats`-style histograms.
4. Remaining procedural tests (timer reload, multiply-long carry, I/O
   read-back) — each is pass/fail and worth ~0.01-0.02 overall.

## Results before this pass (original handoff)

Overall score: **0.3789** (Replay: 0.4606, Procedural: 0.4261, Audio: 0.0865).
See `results/summary.json` for full per-testcase breakdowns.

### Tests passing at 1.0 (perfect match vs Mesen2):
- aw-arm-alu, aw-arm-ldr-str, aw-arm-ldm-stm
- aw-thumb-alu, aw-thumb-ldr-str, aw-thumb-ldm-stm
- memory, dma-priority, mgba-carry, mgba-shifter

### Games running:
- BulletGBA: 0.9934 video SSIM / 0.5645 audio
- Goodboy Advance: 0.9190 video SSIM
- tonc-snd1: 0.9833 video
- Collie Defense: 0.7872 video
- PIU GBA: 0.5011 video
- Waimanu, Spout: running with partial sync

## Known Limitations

1. **Score below baseline** — the 0.53 baseline has tighter edge-case handling on timers and cycle alignment
2. **Timer tests failing** — timer reload/start-stop tests need more precise cycle-level timing of when timer values latch
3. **mgba-multiply-long, mgba-dma** — each has minor flag and open-bus edge cases
4. **ppu-vram-mirror** — VRAM mirroring in the upper 32KB region needs fine-tuning for Mode 3
5. **Replay sync drift** — Celeste, Varooom 3D, and Heartwrench desync after early frames, likely due to subtle interrupt latency or HBlank DMA timing differences
6. **Audio quality is low** — PSG envelope and sweep aren't fully accurate, FIFO sample timing has slight drift

## What I'd Work On Next

In priority order (by expected score impact):

1. **Fix timer latch timing** — timer-reload and timer-start-stop are 0.0; cycle-accurate latching will boost procedural score significantly
2. **HBlank DMA timing** — many gameplay replays desync because DMA doesn't fire at the exact cycle boundaries expected by games
3. **Interrupt delivery latency** — ppu-vram-mirror and game input loops depend on precise IRQ servicing delay
4. **Audio envelope accuracy** — PSG channel sweep/envelope timing affects audio scores across all 9 audio testcases
5. **Prefetch buffer emulation** — some commercial/homebrew titles rely on ROM waitstate prefetch timing

## Features & Subsystems

- **CPU (ARM7TDMI)**: Full implementation of ARM (32-bit) and Thumb (16-bit) instruction sets, barrel shifter, condition evaluation, banked registers, and 3-stage execution pipeline.
- **Memory Bus**: Complete memory mapping for BIOS, EWRAM, IWRAM, I/O registers, Palette RAM, VRAM, OAM, Game Pak ROM, and SRAM with 16-bit bus alignment and open-bus reads.
- **PPU (Graphics)**: 240x160 scanline renderer supporting Modes 0–5 (tiled and bitmap graphics), affine background layers, OAM sprite rendering (affine and regular), windowing, and alpha blending.
- **DMA Controller**: 4 DMA channels with configurable priorities, repeat modes, and audio FIFO streaming triggers.
- **Timers & Interrupts**: 4 hardware timers with cascading prescalers and IRQ generation.
- **APU (Audio)**: PSG channels (square waves, noise, wave RAM) and DirectSound FIFO channels A & B sampled at 32,768 Hz stereo.

# Decision Log & Intermediate Failed Attempts

This document tracks significant design choices, intermediate hypotheses, failed implementations, and how each issue was diagnosed and resolved during development.

---

## 1. Architectural Decisions

### Decision 1: Pure State Encapsulation vs Global Statics
- **Initial Thought**: Use direct `static mut` arrays for ROM, RAM, VRAM, and CPU registers to simplify pointer returns to the C-ABI.
- **Problem**: Caused state pollution across consecutive `emu_reset()` and `emu_load_rom()` cycles, violating test harness determinism.
- **Solution**: Encapsulated the entire system state into an owned struct `Gba` (`src/gba.rs`). The C-ABI in `src/lib.rs` holds a single `Option<Box<Gba>>` that is safely recreated on reset. Large buffers (`rom_buffer`, `audio_buffer`) use heap allocation (`Vec` and `Box`) to avoid stack overflows and static bloat.

### Decision 2: CPU Pipeline Simulation
- **Initial Thought**: Single-cycle instruction fetch and immediate execution without modeling the ARM7TDMI 3-stage fetch-decode-execute pipeline.
- **Problem**: Instructions reading `R15` (PC) obtained incorrect values. In ARM mode, PC is 2 instructions ahead (`+8` bytes); in Thumb mode, it is 2 instructions ahead (`+4` bytes).
- **Solution**: Implemented a 2-instruction pipeline buffer `pipe: [u32; 2]` in `src/cpu/mod.rs`. `flush_pipeline` pre-fills the pipeline on branches/interrupts, and PC increments accurately reflect 3-stage execution.

---

## 2. Failed Attempts & Resolved Bugs

### Bug 1: ARM LDM/STM Block Data Transfer Base Address Drift
- **Symptom**: `aw-arm-ldm-stm` failed completely in early grading runs.
- **Hypothesis**: The register list loop was executing in the wrong order.
- **Root Cause**: For Decrement After (DA) and Decrement Before (DB) addressing modes, the base calculation was subtracting after each store rather than calculating the target memory range upfront, leaving the base register with an improper final offset when writeback was enabled.
- **Fix**: Refactored `exec_block_transfer` in `src/cpu/arm.rs` to compute the low and high memory bounds upfront based on the number of set bits in `r_list`, writing back the correctly computed base pointer.

### Bug 2: Thumb Format 8 (Load/Store Sign-Extended Byte/Halfword) Operand Inversion
- **Symptom**: Thumb memory access tests failed on halfword and sign-extended loads (`aw-thumb-ldr-str`).
- **Hypothesis**: Address offset calculation was wrong.
- **Root Cause**: In opcode bitfield decoding `0x5000 | (h_bit << 11) | (s_bit << 10)`, the conditions for `LDSB` vs `LDRH` had inverted branch checks.
- **Fix**: Re-aligned Thumb opcode masks with the ARM7TDMI reference manual, correcting `LDSB`, `LDRH`, and `LDSH` decoding.

### Bug 3: 8-bit / 16-bit MMIO Bus Routing & Open-Bus Reads
- **Symptom**: `mgba-io-read` returned mismatched values on 8-bit reads from 16-bit registers.
- **Hypothesis**: MMIO registers needed dedicated 8-bit read matches for all addresses.
- **Root Cause**: GBA IO registers are physically connected to a 16-bit bus. Reading an odd byte from a 16-bit register returns bits 8..15 of that register, not zero or unmapped memory. Unmapped registers also return the internal bus open-bus value rather than 0x00.
- **Fix**: Refactored `read_io8` in `src/bus/mod.rs` to delegate to `read_io16(addr & !1)` and extract the requested byte. Added proper open-bus masking for write-only registers (e.g. DMA controls, sound FIFOs).

### Bug 4: Register-Specified Shifts with R15 (PC) Prefetch Delta
- **Symptom**: Arithmetic and logical shifts using a register operand (`LSL Rs`, `ASR Rs`) produced incorrect results when `Rs = R15` or `Rm = R15`.
- **Hypothesis**: ALU shift logic was mishandling shift counts ≥ 32.
- **Root Cause**: On ARM7TDMI, when a register-specified shift is used, an internal cycle is spent reading the shift amount. During this extra cycle, the PC has advanced an extra instruction (+12 instead of +8).
- **Fix**: Updated `src/cpu/arm.rs` so that register-specified shifts treat `R15` operand reads as PC + 12 (Commit `5fd7684`).

---

## 3. Preserved Known Limitations (Active Backlog)

1. **Timer Latching Edge Cases**: The reload and start/stop latch latency currently does not match sub-cycle timing, causing `timer-reload` and `timer-start-stop` to fail.
2. **HBlank DMA Cycle Alignment**: HBlank DMA fires at scanline boundary instead of exact cycle 1006, causing replay desync in games that perform palette swaps mid-scanline.
3. **APU PSG Sweep & Envelope Accuracy**: Sound channel envelopes currently step on simplified intervals rather than cycle-exact 64Hz/256Hz dividers, resulting in low audio log-mel scores.

# Independent Reproduction & Grading Guide

This document provides step-by-step instructions to independently compile, verify, and grade the WebAssembly GBA emulator (`gba_emu`) against the Mechanize GBA Eval benchmark.

rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown

## 5. Native grading without Docker (used for the 2026-11-07 timing/audio pass)

The numbers in `HANDOFF.md` for the timing/audio pass were produced with a
native grader build, not Docker. Steps on a fresh Ubuntu host:

```bash

85	| **Final** (`dist/gba_emu.wasm`, sha256 b2705a31…) | **0.6900** | **0.7181** | **0.5861** | **0.7096** |

89	
90	### What was wrong (root causes found)
91	1. **Timing model unused.** A waitstate table existed but no instruction
92	   was ever charged memory waitstates; every instruction cost a fixed 1-3
93	   cycles, so games ran several times too fast relative to the PPU.
94	2. **HALT never halted.** HALTCNT was stored but the CPU kept running.
95	3. **APU clocked for the Game Boy, not the GBA.** Square/wave/noise timers
96	   used GB multipliers (pitch 4x too high), the frame sequencer
97	   (length/envelope/sweep) did not exist, and timers advanced at most one
98	   step per call. tonc-snd1 audio went 0.10 → 1.00 after the rewrite.
99	4. **Branch detection bug.** `step()` decided "no branch" by comparing r15
100	   before/after; a BX to the next word or `b .` refills to the same r15,
101	   so an extra ARM word was fetched. chip-advance hung in its crt0 because
102	   of this (video 0.03 before).
103	5. **Frame boundary and boot alignment.** The reference ends frames at
104	   VBlank start and reports 6 boot frames (`emu_boot_frames`); we ended
105	   frames at line 0 and reported 0, so every replay was phase-shifted.
106	6. **Input applied one frame early.** The reference latches keys at the
107	   frame boundary; we applied them immediately (goodboy: 840 → 48
108	   differing frames of 900).
109	7. **Fixed 32768 Hz output.** Games selecting 65536 Hz via SOUNDBIAS get
110	   twice the samples from the reference; the grader compares streams
111	   sample-for-sample (piugba audio 0.06 → 0.70).
112	8. **Mosaic not implemented; darken rounding off by one** (chip-advance
113	   fades).
114	9. Many smaller hardware rules (VRAM mirror hole in bitmap modes, open
115	   bus = last prefetched opcode, BIOS read protection, ROM out-of-range
116	   reads, DMA masks/latch/ROM-increment, DISPSTAT byte writes clearing
117	   status bits, PPU lagging one scanline per call after long DMAs,
118	   write-only DMA registers reading 0, timer start/stop latency).
119	
120	### Method
121	- Baseline first, then every change validated with the real grader
122	  (`tools/quick-grade.sh` on subsets, `tools/grade.sh` for full runs).
123	- **Instruction-level lockstep against the reference** (`tools/lockstep`):
124	  runs `reference/mesen.wasm` one instruction at a time beside our core and
125	  reports the first PC/cycle divergence with per-access logs. This turned
126	  timing work from guesswork into measurement; see `docs/TIMING_MODEL.md`
127	  for every rule and its evidence. goodboy-advance now runs 8M+
128	  instructions in exact PC lockstep.
129	- Regression tests for each fixed bug: `tests/regressions.rs`.
130	
131	### Known limitations after this pass
132	See `docs/TIMING_MODEL.md` "Known gaps": PPU/CPU VRAM contention not
133	modelled, prefetch-buffer and DMA edge cases (±1 cycle), a few IRQ
134	boundaries, timer reload-while-running, multiply-long carry flag,
135	mgba-io-read (48/130), mgba-dma (1248/1256).
136	
137	### What I'd do next
138	1. Model VRAM/palette/OAM contention from the PPU's fetch schedule (the
139	   tracer's `--vram-stats` gives the target histogram). This is now the
140	   largest source of drift in mode-0 games.
141	2. Fit the remaining IRQ sampling rule with `--irq-report` data across
142	   all games.
143	3. Finish prefetch/DMA edge cases with `--branch-stats`-style histograms.
144	4. Remaining procedural tests (timer reload, multiply-long carry, I/O
145	   read-back) — each is pass/fail and worth ~0.01-0.02 overall.

241	## Features & Subsystems
242	
243	- **CPU (ARM7TDMI)**: Full implementation of ARM (32-bit) and Thumb (16-bit) instruction sets, barrel shifter, condition evaluation, banked registers, and 3-stage execution pipeline.
244	- **Memory Bus**: Complete memory mapping for BIOS, EWRAM, IWRAM, I/O registers, Palette RAM, VRAM, OAM, Game Pak ROM, and SRAM with 16-bit bus alignment and open-bus reads.
245	- **PPU (Graphics)**: 240x160 scanline renderer supporting Modes 0–5 (tiled and bitmap graphics), affine background layers, OAM sprite rendering (affine and regular), windowing, and alpha blending.
246	- **DMA Controller**: 4 DMA channels with configurable priorities, repeat modes, and audio FIFO streaming triggers.
247	- **Timers & Interrupts**: 4 hardware timers with cascading prescalers and IRQ generation.
248	- **APU (Audio)**: PSG channels (square waves, noise, wave RAM) and DirectSound FIFO channels A & B sampled at 32,768 Hz stereo.

338	# Decision Log & Intermediate Failed Attempts
339	
340	This document tracks significant design choices, intermediate hypotheses, failed implementations, and how each issue was diagnosed and resolved during development.
341	
342	---
343	
344	## 1. Architectural Decisions
345	
346	### Decision 1: Pure State Encapsulation vs Global Statics
347	- **Initial Thought**: Use direct `static mut` arrays for ROM, RAM, VRAM, and CPU registers to simplify pointer returns to the C-ABI.
348	- **Problem**: Caused state pollution across consecutive `emu_reset()` and `emu_load_rom()` cycles, violating test harness determinism.
349	- **Solution**: Encapsulated the entire system state into an owned struct `Gba` (`src/gba.rs`). The C-ABI in `src/lib.rs` holds a single `Option<Box<Gba>>` that is safely recreated on reset. Large buffers (`rom_buffer`, `audio_buffer`) use heap allocation (`Vec` and `Box`) to avoid stack overflows and static bloat.
350	
351	### Decision 2: CPU Pipeline Simulation
352	- **Initial Thought**: Single-cycle instruction fetch and immediate execution without modeling the ARM7TDMI 3-stage fetch-decode-execute pipeline.
353	- **Problem**: Instructions reading `R15` (PC) obtained incorrect values. In ARM mode, PC is 2 instructions ahead (`+8` bytes); in Thumb mode, it is 2 instructions ahead (`+4` bytes).
354	- **Solution**: Implemented a 2-instruction pipeline buffer `pipe: [u32; 2]` in `src/cpu/mod.rs`. `flush_pipeline` pre-fills the pipeline on branches/interrupts, and PC increments accurately reflect 3-stage execution.
355	
356	---
357	
358	## 2. Failed Attempts & Resolved Bugs
359	
360	### Bug 1: ARM LDM/STM Block Data Transfer Base Address Drift
361	- **Symptom**: `aw-arm-ldm-stm` failed completely in early grading runs.
362	- **Hypothesis**: The register list loop was executing in the wrong order.
363	- **Root Cause**: For Decrement After (DA) and Decrement Before (DB) addressing modes, the base calculation was subtracting after each store rather than calculating the target memory range upfront, leaving the base register with an improper final offset when writeback was enabled.
364	- **Fix**: Refactored `exec_block_transfer` in `src/cpu/arm.rs` to compute the low and high memory bounds upfront based on the number of set bits in `r_list`, writing back the correctly computed base pointer.
365	
366	### Bug 2: Thumb Format 8 (Load/Store Sign-Extended Byte/Halfword) Operand Inversion
367	- **Symptom**: Thumb memory access tests failed on halfword and sign-extended loads (`aw-thumb-ldr-str`).
368	- **Hypothesis**: Address offset calculation was wrong.
369	- **Root Cause**: In opcode bitfield decoding `0x5000 | (h_bit << 11) | (s_bit << 10)`, the conditions for `LDSB` vs `LDRH` had inverted branch checks.
370	- **Fix**: Re-aligned Thumb opcode masks with the ARM7TDMI reference manual, correcting `LDSB`, `LDRH`, and `LDSH` decoding.
371	
372	### Bug 3: 8-bit / 16-bit MMIO Bus Routing & Open-Bus Reads
373	- **Symptom**: `mgba-io-read` returned mismatched values on 8-bit reads from 16-bit registers.
374	- **Hypothesis**: MMIO registers needed dedicated 8-bit read matches for all addresses.
375	- **Root Cause**: GBA IO registers are physically connected to a 16-bit bus. Reading an odd byte from a 16-bit register returns bits 8..15 of that register, not zero or unmapped memory. Unmapped registers also return the internal bus open-bus value rather than 0x00.
376	- **Fix**: Refactored `read_io8` in `src/bus/mod.rs` to delegate to `read_io16(addr & !1)` and extract the requested byte. Added proper open-bus masking for write-only registers (e.g. DMA controls, sound FIFOs).
377	
378	### Bug 4: Register-Specified Shifts with R15 (PC) Prefetch Delta
379	- **Symptom**: Arithmetic and logical shifts using a register operand (`LSL Rs`, `ASR Rs`) produced incorrect results when `Rs = R15` or `Rm = R15`.
380	- **Hypothesis**: ALU shift logic was mishandling shift counts ≥ 32.
381	- **Root Cause**: On ARM7TDMI, when a register-specified shift is used, an internal cycle is spent reading the shift amount. During this extra cycle, the PC has advanced an extra instruction (+12 instead of +8).
382	- **Fix**: Updated `src/cpu/arm.rs` so that register-specified shifts treat `R15` operand reads as PC + 12 (Commit `5fd7684`).
383

389	2. **HBlank DMA Cycle Alignment**: HBlank DMA fires at scanline boundary instead of exact cycle 1006, causing replay desync in games that perform palette swaps mid-scanline.

# Handoff: GBA Emulator (agbrs)

## Overview

Original Game Boy Advance emulator built from scratch in Rust, targeting `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Implements all major GBA hardware subsystems: ARM7TDMI CPU (ARM + Thumb), memory bus, PPU, DMA, timers, interrupts, and audio (PSG + DirectSound FIFO).

## Approach

### Phase 1: Research & scaffold
Read through GBATEK and the ABI spec. Set up the Cargo project with correct `cdylib` crate type and the 10 required C-ABI exports. Got a blank wasm compiling first before writing any emulation logic.

### Phase 2: CPU + Memory (highest leverage)
Implemented the ARM7TDMI with all data processing, multiply, single/block transfer, and branch instructions for both ARM and Thumb modes. Built the memory bus with correct address mapping for all GBA regions (BIOS, EWRAM, IWRAM, IO, Palette, VRAM, OAM, ROM, SRAM). Loaded the provided BIOS stub at 0x00000000.

Key decisions:
- 3-stage pipeline model: PC always reads as current_instruction + 8 (ARM) or + 4 (Thumb)
- Wrapping arithmetic everywhere to satisfy the zero-panic policy
- Open-bus reads for unmapped regions instead of crashing
- 16-bit IO bus routing: `read_io8` delegates to `read_io16` and extracts the right byte

### Phase 3: PPU
Scanline-based renderer running at cycle 960 (end of HDRAW). Supports:
- Modes 0-2 (tiled backgrounds with regular and affine layers)
- Modes 3-5 (bitmap modes)
- OAM sprites (regular and affine, all sizes)
- Windowing (WIN0, WIN1, OBJ window)
- Alpha blending and brightness effects
- Priority-based layer compositing

### Phase 4: DMA, Timers, Audio
- 4 DMA channels with priority ordering and audio FIFO triggers
- 4 cascading timers with prescaler dividers
- PSG channels 1-4 (square waves, wave RAM, noise)
- DirectSound FIFO A and B at 32768 Hz stereo

### Phase 5: Debug & iterate
Used the grader and oracle tools to identify failing tests and fix specific issues:
- LDM/STM block transfer had wrong base address calculation for DA/DB modes
- Thumb Format 8 had swapped operands (LDSB vs LDRH)
- IO register reads needed 16-bit bus alignment
- DMA registers returned wrong open-bus values
- Register-specified shifts needed PC+12 for R15 reads

## Architecture

```
src/
├── lib.rs          # WASM ABI exports (10 C-ABI functions)
├── gba.rs          # Top-level Gba struct, frame loop
├── cpu/
│   ├── mod.rs      # Pipeline, mode switching, interrupt handling
│   ├── arm.rs      # ARM instruction decoder/executor
│   ├── thumb.rs    # Thumb instruction decoder/executor
│   ├── alu.rs      # ALU operations with flag computation
│   └── registers.rs # Banked register definitions
├── bus/
│   ├── mod.rs      # Memory map, read/write dispatch
│   ├── io.rs       # IO register bitfield constants
│   └── waitstates.rs # ROM waitstate configuration
├── ppu/
│   └── mod.rs      # Scanline renderer, all BG modes, sprites
├── dma/
│   └── mod.rs      # 4-channel DMA controller
├── timer/
│   └── mod.rs      # 4 cascading timers
└── apu/
    └── mod.rs      # PSG + DirectSound FIFO audio
```

Total: ~4,500 lines of Rust.

## 2026-11-07 pass: timing, audio and differential testing

This pass was done with Claude Code (model: Claude Opus 5.5) driven by the
repository owner. Goal: check the repo against the take-home requirements,
find why the score was low, and raise it with validated changes.

### Score (gba-eval grader, native build, reference = bundled Mesen2)

| Run | Overall | Replay (60%) | Procedural (20%) | Audio (20%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (`dist/` wasm at commit e549c6a) | 0.3789 | 0.4606 | 0.4261 | 0.0865 |
| Intermediate (v8: APU rewrite, access timing, frame/boot alignment) | 0.5655 | 0.5537 | 0.5861 | 0.5802 |
| v11 (+ lockstep-derived IRQ/DMA/prefetch rules, input latching) | 0.6775 | 0.7137 | 0.5861 | 0.6605 |
| **Final** (`dist/gba_emu.wasm`, sha256 b2705a31…) | **0.6900** | **0.7181** | **0.5861** | **0.7096** |

Per-testcase tables: `results/` (baseline, v8, final), produced by
`tools/scores.py`.

### What was wrong (root causes found)
1. **Timing model unused.** A waitstate table existed but no instruction
   was ever charged memory waitstates; every instruction cost a fixed 1-3
   cycles, so games ran several times too fast relative to the PPU.
2. **HALT never halted.** HALTCNT was stored but the CPU kept running.
3. **APU clocked for the Game Boy, not the GBA.** Square/wave/noise timers
   used GB multipliers (pitch 4x too high), the frame sequencer
   (length/envelope/sweep) did not exist, and timers advanced at most one
   step per call. tonc-snd1 audio went 0.10 → 1.00 after the rewrite.
4. **Branch detection bug.** `step()` decided "no branch" by comparing r15
   before/after; a BX to the next word or `b .` refills to the same r15,
   so an extra ARM word was fetched. chip-advance hung in its crt0 because
   of this (video 0.03 before).
5. **Frame boundary and boot alignment.** The reference ends frames at
   VBlank start and reports 6 boot frames (`emu_boot_frames`); we ended
   frames at line 0 and reported 0, so every replay was phase-shifted.
6. **Input applied one frame early.** The reference latches keys at the
   frame boundary; we applied them immediately (goodboy: 840 → 48
   differing frames of 900).
7. **Fixed 32768 Hz output.** Games selecting 65536 Hz via SOUNDBIAS get
   twice the samples from the reference; the grader compares streams
   sample-for-sample (piugba audio 0.06 → 0.70).
8. **Mosaic not implemented; darken rounding off by one** (chip-advance
   fades).
9. Many smaller hardware rules (VRAM mirror hole in bitmap modes, open
   bus = last prefetched opcode, BIOS read protection, ROM out-of-range
   reads, DMA masks/latch/ROM-increment, DISPSTAT byte writes clearing
   status bits, PPU lagging one scanline per call after long DMAs,
   write-only DMA registers reading 0, timer start/stop latency).

### Method
- Baseline first, then every change validated with the real grader
  (`tools/quick-grade.sh` on subsets, `tools/grade.sh` for full runs).
- **Instruction-level lockstep against the reference** (`tools/lockstep`):
  runs `reference/mesen.wasm` one instruction at a time beside our core and
  reports the first PC/cycle divergence with per-access logs. This turned
  timing work from guesswork into measurement; see `docs/TIMING_MODEL.md`
  for every rule and its evidence. goodboy-advance now runs 8M+
  instructions in exact PC lockstep.
- Regression tests for each fixed bug: `tests/regressions.rs`.

### Known limitations after this pass
See `docs/TIMING_MODEL.md` "Known gaps": PPU/CPU VRAM contention not
modelled, prefetch-buffer and DMA edge cases (±1 cycle), a few IRQ
boundaries, timer reload-while-running, multiply-long carry flag,
mgba-io-read (48/130), mgba-dma (1248/1256).

### What I'd do next
1. Model VRAM/palette/OAM contention from the PPU's fetch schedule (the
   tracer's `--vram-stats` gives the target histogram). This is now the
   largest source of drift in mode-0 games.
2. Fit the remaining IRQ sampling rule with `--irq-report` data across
   all games.
3. Finish prefetch/DMA edge cases with `--branch-stats`-style histograms.
4. Remaining procedural tests (timer reload, multiply-long carry, I/O
   read-back) — each is pass/fail and worth ~0.01-0.02 overall.

## Results before this pass (original handoff)

Overall score: **0.3789** (Replay: 0.4606, Procedural: 0.4261, Audio: 0.0865).
See `results/summary.json` for full per-testcase breakdowns.

### Tests passing at 1.0 (perfect match vs Mesen2):
- aw-arm-alu, aw-arm-ldr-str, aw-arm-ldm-stm
- aw-thumb-alu, aw-thumb-ldr-str, aw-thumb-ldm-stm
- memory, dma-priority, mgba-carry, mgba-shifter

### Games running:
- BulletGBA: 0.9934 video SSIM / 0.5645 audio
- Goodboy Advance: 0.9190 video SSIM
- tonc-snd1: 0.9833 video
- Collie Defense: 0.7872 video
- PIU GBA: 0.5011 video
- Waimanu, Spout: running with partial sync

## Known Limitations

1. **Score below baseline** — the 0.53 baseline has tighter edge-case handling on timers and cycle alignment
2. **Timer tests failing** — timer reload/start-stop tests need more precise cycle-level timing of when timer values latch
3. **mgba-multiply-long, mgba-dma** — each has minor flag and open-bus edge cases
4. **ppu-vram-mirror** — VRAM mirroring in the upper 32KB region needs fine-tuning for Mode 3
5. **Replay sync drift** — Celeste, Varooom 3D, and Heartwrench desync after early frames, likely due to subtle interrupt latency or HBlank DMA timing differences
6. **Audio quality is low** — PSG envelope and sweep aren't fully accurate, FIFO sample timing has slight drift

## What I'd Work On Next

In priority order (by expected score impact):

1. **Fix timer latch timing** — timer-reload and timer-start-stop are 0.0; cycle-accurate latching will boost procedural score significantly
2. **HBlank DMA timing** — many gameplay replays desync because DMA doesn't fire at the exact cycle boundaries expected by games
3. **Interrupt delivery latency** — ppu-vram-mirror and game input loops depend on precise IRQ servicing delay
4. **Audio envelope accuracy** — PSG channel sweep/envelope timing affects audio scores across all 9 audio testcases
5. **Prefetch buffer emulation** — some commercial/homebrew titles rely on ROM waitstate prefetch timing

## Build & Grade

See [`docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md`](docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md) for complete instructions.

```bash
# build
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown

# the wasm output
ls target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm

# grade (requires gba-eval repo)
cd /path/to/gba-eval
./quickstart/grade.sh /path/to/agbrs/dist/gba_emu.wasm my-run
cat results/my-run/summary.json
```

## AI Orchestration & Process Deliverables

Detailed logs, prompts, and failure records requested for the evaluation handoff:
- **Reproduction Guide**: [`docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md`](docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md)
- **Decisions & Failed Attempts**: [`docs/DECISIONS_AND_FAILURES.md`](docs/DECISIONS_AND_FAILURES.md)
- **Workflow & Environment Metadata**: [`docs/WORKFLOW_METADATA.md`](docs/WORKFLOW_METADATA.md)
- **Agent Prompts & Transcripts**: [`agent/antigravity/`](agent/antigravity/)
- **Compiled WASM Artifact**: [`dist/gba_emu.wasm`](dist/gba_emu.wasm)

## Tools Used

- **Editor & Orchestration**: Google DeepMind Antigravity framework
- **AI Models**: Claude 3.5 Sonnet / Gemini 1.5 Pro / Claude Opus for implementation guidance, debugging, and code review
- **Reference**: GBATEK (Martin Korth), ARM7TDMI datasheet, gba-eval oracle tool
- **Testing**: gba-eval grader + oracle for differential frame comparison against Mesen2
# GBA Emulator (Rust / WebAssembly)

An original Game Boy Advance (GBA) emulator written in Rust from scratch, compiled to WebAssembly (`wasm32-unknown-unknown`) for the [Mechanize GBA Eval](https://github.com/mechanize-work/gba-eval) benchmark.

---

## 📋 Evaluation & Handoff Deliverables

All deliverables requested for the engineering trial are documented and organized in this repository:

| Deliverable | Location | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Executive Handoff** | [HANDOFF.md](HANDOFF.md) | Architectural overview, benchmark results (baseline 0.3789 → see the 2026-11-07 pass), and limitations |
| **Compiled Artifact** | [dist/gba_emu.wasm](dist/gba_emu.wasm) | Pre-built, verified release WebAssembly binary (85 KB) |
| **Reproduction Guide** | [docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md](docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md) | Step-by-step instructions to rebuild, run unit tests, and grade against Mesen2 |
| **Decisions & Failures** | [docs/DECISIONS_AND_FAILURES.md](docs/DECISIONS_AND_FAILURES.md) | Log of intermediate design pivots, failed attempts, and bug diagnoses |
| **Workflow Metadata** | [docs/WORKFLOW_METADATA.md](docs/WORKFLOW_METADATA.md) | Toolchain versions (Rust 1.99.1), human time spent (13.5 hrs), and model usage |
| **AI Agent Configs** | [agent/antigravity/](agent/antigravity/) | Prompts, subagent configurations, and filtered engineering conversations |
| **Benchmark Output** | [results/](results/) | `summary.json` + per-test `scores.txt` for the baseline, intermediate and final runs (all 27 testcases) |
| **Timing model** | [docs/TIMING_MODEL.md](docs/TIMING_MODEL.md) | Cycle-timing rules derived by instruction-level lockstep against the reference, with evidence and known gaps |
| **Dev tools** | [tools/](tools/), [examples/run.rs](examples/run.rs) | Native grading scripts, lockstep tracer vs Mesen2, frame/audio diff tools, native debug runner |

---

## Features & Subsystems

- **CPU (ARM7TDMI)**: Full implementation of ARM (32-bit) and Thumb (16-bit) instruction sets, barrel shifter, condition evaluation, banked registers, and 3-stage execution pipeline.
- **Memory Bus**: Complete memory mapping for BIOS, EWRAM, IWRAM, I/O registers, Palette RAM, VRAM, OAM, Game Pak ROM, and SRAM with 16-bit bus alignment and open-bus reads.
- **PPU (Graphics)**: 240x160 scanline renderer supporting Modes 0–5 (tiled and bitmap graphics), affine background layers, OAM sprite rendering (affine and regular), windowing, and alpha blending.
- **DMA Controller**: 4 DMA channels with configurable priorities, repeat modes, and audio FIFO streaming triggers.
- **Timers & Interrupts**: 4 hardware timers with cascading prescalers and IRQ generation.
- **APU (Audio)**: PSG channels (square waves, noise, wave RAM) and DirectSound FIFO channels A & B sampled at 32,768 Hz stereo.

---

## Quickstart: Building & Testing

### 1. Build WebAssembly Binary
```bash
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
```
Output: `target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm` (or use pre-built `dist/gba_emu.wasm`).

### 2. Run Tests
```bash
cargo test
```

### 3. Grade with GBA Eval
```bash
./quickstart/grade.sh dist/gba_emu.wasm my-run
```
See [docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md](docs/REPRODUCIBILITY.md) for full grading details.

---

## Standard C-ABI Exports

The WebAssembly core exports the standard 10 C-ABI functions:
- `emu_init() -> i32`
- `emu_rom_buffer() -> *mut u8`
- `emu_load_rom(len: i32) -> i32`
- `emu_reset() -> i32`
- `emu_set_keys(keys: u32)`
- `emu_run_frame()`
- `emu_framebuffer() -> *const u32`
- `emu_audio_buffer() -> *const i16`
- `emu_audio_samples() -> i32`
- `emu_audio_rate() -> i32`

| **Phase 2: Core Subsystems** | 4.0 hrs | ARM7TDMI (ARM/Thumb), registers, condition flags, MMIO bus mapping |
| **Phase 3: Hardware Peripherals** | 3.5 hrs | PPU scanline renderer (Modes 0-5), DMA controller, Timers, APU |
| **Phase 4: Debugging & Grader Iteration** | 3.0 hrs | Oracle differential tracing, fixing LDM/STM and shift prefetch, test execution |

# Decision Log & Intermediate Failed Attempts

This document tracks significant design choices, intermediate hypotheses, failed implementations, and how each issue was diagnosed and resolved during development.

---

## 1. Architectural Decisions

### Decision 1: Pure State Encapsulation vs Global Statics
- **Initial Thought**: Use direct `static mut` arrays for ROM, RAM, VRAM, and CPU registers to simplify pointer returns to the C-ABI.
- **Problem**: Caused state pollution across consecutive `emu_reset()` and `emu_load_rom()` cycles, violating test harness determinism.
- **Solution**: Encapsulated the entire system state into an owned struct `Gba` (`src/gba.rs`). The C-ABI in `src/lib.rs` holds a single `Option<Box<Gba>>` that is safely recreated on reset. Large buffers (`rom_buffer`, `audio_buffer`) use heap allocation (`Vec` and `Box`) to avoid stack overflows and static bloat.

### Decision 2: CPU Pipeline Simulation
- **Initial Thought**: Single-cycle instruction fetch and immediate execution without modeling the ARM7TDMI 3-stage fetch-decode-execute pipeline.
- **Problem**: Instructions reading `R15` (PC) obtained incorrect values. In ARM mode, PC is 2 instructions ahead (`+8` bytes); in Thumb mode, it is 2 instructions ahead (`+4` bytes).
- **Solution**: Implemented a 2-instruction pipeline buffer `pipe: [u32; 2]` in `src/cpu/mod.rs`. `flush_pipeline` pre-fills the pipeline on branches/interrupts, and PC increments accurately reflect 3-stage execution.

---

## 2. Failed Attempts & Resolved Bugs

### Bug 1: ARM LDM/STM Block Data Transfer Base Address Drift
- **Symptom**: `aw-arm-ldm-stm` failed completely in early grading runs.
- **Hypothesis**: The register list loop was executing in the wrong order.
- **Root Cause**: For Decrement After (DA) and Decrement Before (DB) addressing modes, the base calculation was subtracting after each store rather than calculating the target memory range upfront, leaving the base register with an improper final offset when writeback was enabled.
- **Fix**: Refactored `exec_block_transfer` in `src/cpu/arm.rs` to compute the low and high memory bounds upfront based on the number of set bits in `r_list`, writing back the correctly computed base pointer.

### Bug 2: Thumb Format 8 (Load/Store Sign-Extended Byte/Halfword) Operand Inversion
- **Symptom**: Thumb memory access tests failed on halfword and sign-extended loads (`aw-thumb-ldr-str`).
- **Hypothesis**: Address offset calculation was wrong.
- **Root Cause**: In opcode bitfield decoding `0x5000 | (h_bit << 11) | (s_bit << 10)`, the conditions for `LDSB` vs `LDRH` had inverted branch checks.
- **Fix**: Re-aligned Thumb opcode masks with the ARM7TDMI reference manual, correcting `LDSB`, `LDRH`, and `LDSH` decoding.

### Bug 3: 8-bit / 16-bit MMIO Bus Routing & Open-Bus Reads
- **Symptom**: `mgba-io-read` returned mismatched values on 8-bit reads from 16-bit registers.
- **Hypothesis**: MMIO registers needed dedicated 8-bit read matches for all addresses.
- **Root Cause**: GBA IO registers are physically connected to a 16-bit bus. Reading an odd byte from a 16-bit register returns bits 8..15 of that register, not zero or unmapped memory. Unmapped registers also return the internal bus open-bus value rather than 0x00.
- **Fix**: Refactored `read_io8` in `src/bus/mod.rs` to delegate to `read_io16(addr & !1)` and extract the requested byte. Added proper open-bus masking for write-only registers (e.g. DMA controls, sound FIFOs).

### Bug 4: Register-Specified Shifts with R15 (PC) Prefetch Delta
- **Symptom**: Arithmetic and logical shifts using a register operand (`LSL Rs`, `ASR Rs`) produced incorrect results when `Rs = R15` or `Rm = R15`.
- **Hypothesis**: ALU shift logic was mishandling shift counts ≥ 32.
- **Root Cause**: On ARM7TDMI, when a register-specified shift is used, an internal cycle is spent reading the shift amount. During this extra cycle, the PC has advanced an extra instruction (+12 instead of +8).
- **Fix**: Updated `src/cpu/arm.rs` so that register-specified shifts treat `R15` operand reads as PC + 12 (Commit `5fd7684`).

---

## 3. Preserved Known Limitations (Active Backlog)

1. **Timer Latching Edge Cases**: The reload and start/stop latch latency currently does not match sub-cycle timing, causing `timer-reload` and `timer-start-stop` to fail.
2. **HBlank DMA Cycle Alignment**: HBlank DMA fires at scanline boundary instead of exact cycle 1006, causing replay desync in games that perform palette swaps mid-scanline.
3. **APU PSG Sweep & Envelope Accuracy**: Sound channel envelopes currently step on simplified intervals rather than cycle-exact 64Hz/256Hz dividers, resulting in low audio log-mel scores.

# Independent Reproduction & Grading Guide

This document provides step-by-step instructions to independently compile, verify, and grade the WebAssembly GBA emulator (`gba_emu`) against the Mechanize GBA Eval benchmark.

---

## 1. Prerequisites & Toolchain

The emulator core is written in pure Rust (edition 2021) with zero third-party crate dependencies to ensure deterministic compilation and zero host-level vulnerabilities.

- **Rust**: 1.80+ (Tested on `rustc 1.99.1`)
- **Cargo**: Corresponding version (Tested on `cargo 1.99.1`)
- **Wasm Target**: `wasm32-unknown-unknown`
- **Harness Environment**: Linux x86_64, Git LFS (for reference caches), Docker / Wasmtime

### Install Target
```bash
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
```

---

## 2. Compiling the WebAssembly Binary

From the repository root:

```bash
cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
```

The compiled release artifact will be output to:
```
target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm
```

A pre-built, verified release binary matching the benchmark run is also provided at:
```
dist/gba_emu.wasm
```

### Verification (SHA-256)
You can verify the candidate binary hash:
```bash
sha256sum target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm
```

---

## 3. Running Unit & Integration Tests

The repository includes sanity and smoke test harnesses:

```bash
cargo test
```

Expected output:
```
running 1 test
test test_smoke ... ok
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored
```

---

## 4. Grading with Mechanize GBA Eval

To evaluate the emulator against the full 27-testcase reference corpus using `Mesen2`:

1. Clone and initialize the `gba-eval` evaluation harness repository:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/mechanize-work/gba-eval.git
cd gba-eval

# Initialize submodules and pull precomputed reference caches
git submodule update --init --recursive
git lfs install && git lfs pull
```

2. Run pre-flight check:
```bash
./quickstart/smoke-test.sh
```

3. Run the automated grading suite on the candidate binary:
```bash
./quickstart/grade.sh /path/to/agbrs/dist/gba_emu.wasm submission-run
```

4. Inspect the resulting metrics and screenshot diffs:
```bash
cat results/submission-run/summary.json
```

The output JSON includes the composite overall score, sub-scores for Replay, Procedural, and Audio, as well as per-testcase breakdowns.


---

## 5. Native grading without Docker (used for the 2026-11-07 timing/audio pass)

The numbers in `HANDOFF.md` for the timing/audio pass were produced with a
native grader build, not Docker. Steps on a fresh Ubuntu host:

```bash
# toolchain
curl -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --profile minimal --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
sudo apt-get install -y build-essential git-lfs     # grader needs a C linker

# eval harness, next to this repo (tools/ default to ../gba-eval)
git clone https://github.com/mechanize-work/gba-eval.git ../gba-eval
(cd ../gba-eval && git lfs install && git lfs pull && cargo build -p grader --release)

# build + grade
cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
tools/grade.sh target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm my-run 1
python3 tools/scores.py ../gba-eval/results/my-run            # per-test table
```

Memory: each grader worker holds two emulator instances plus reference
caches. On an 8 GB host, `RAYON_NUM_THREADS` > 2 was OOM-killed; the
`tools/grade.sh` third argument sets the thread count (1 thread ≈ 28 min
for all 27 testcases, 2 threads ≈ 15 min).

### Fast iteration on a subset
```bash
tools/quick-grade.sh <wasm> <run-name> timer-reload ppu-vram-mirror tonc-snd1
```
Builds a filtered corpus view (symlinks + filtered `testcases.json`) so the
real grader and reference caches are used unchanged.

### Debugging tools (not part of the wasm)
| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `cargo run --release --example run -- <rom> <frames> [--replay f] [--dump dir] [--wav f] [--trace-frame n] [--watch addr] [--peek addr] [--steps n]` | native runner: per-frame state, PPM frames, WAV, instruction trace, watchpoints |
| `tools/lockstep` (`CARGO_TARGET_DIR=../gba-eval/target cargo build --release` inside it) | instruction-level lockstep vs `reference/mesen.wasm`; see `docs/TIMING_MODEL.md` |
| `tools/firstdiff.py`, `tools/ppm2png.py` | first divergent frame between oracle and our PPM dumps; side-by-side PNG with diff mask |
| `tools/wavcmp.py`, `tools/audiolag.py` | level/pitch comparison and windowed waveform cross-correlation (needs numpy) |

Oracle frames/audio: `ORACLE_MESEN_WASM=../gba-eval/reference/mesen.wasm ../gba-eval/target/release/oracle run <rom> <frames> [--replay f] --dump-frames dir --dump-audio f.wav`.
Note: the oracle CLI does not drain audio during its 6 boot frames and the
reference's buffer caps at 2048 pairs, so its WAV is missing ~1086 samples
at the start compared with what the grader sees. Skip 2048 samples (not
6 frames' worth) when aligning against our `--wav` output.

### Unit / regression tests
```bash
cargo test --release
```
`tests/regressions.rs` pins down behaviours fixed in the timing/audio pass
(branch-to-same-PC pipeline bug, HALT, VRAM mirror hole, ROM open bus,
BIOS read protection, PSG pitch, timer start/stop latency).

# GBA Eval

We give frontier AI coding agents 24 hours to write a complete software GBA emulator with WebAssembly support. We grade the emulators they produce against Mesen2, one of the most accurate software GBA emulators available.

GBA Eval is analogous to the work [Mechanize](https://mechanize.work) does with top AI labs when we make environments for evaluating and training frontier LLMs, and we hope it gives a concrete sense of what we mean when we talk about environments and grading. If designing and building high-quality evaluations sounds like something you'd want to do, we're [hiring software engineers](https://mechanize.work/apply/software-engineer/?utm_source=gba-eval&utm_campaign=gba-eval).

## See the attempts

The nine emulators produced by the May 2026 leaderboard lineup —
their full commit-by-commit autosave history and a rendered chat-log
transcript for each — are published at
[mechanize-work/gba-eval-attempts](https://github.com/mechanize-work/gba-eval-attempts).
Each model has its own subrepo so you can clone just the one you're
interested in.

## Quickstart

Grade a wasm, or run your own agent inside the benchmark's container.
Docker is the only required dep.

```bash
git submodule update --init --recursive
git lfs install && git lfs pull

./quickstart/smoke-test.sh                                          # 30s preflight
./quickstart/grade.sh candidates/gba-core/gba_core_shim.wasm baseline
```

See [`quickstart/README.md`](quickstart/README.md) for the full
walkthrough — running your own agent in the container, grading a
wasm your agent produced with `--from-container`, and the `--native`
path that skips docker.

## How grading works

```bash
# One-time: precompute reference frames + per-replay thresholds.
# Writes corpus/reference-cache/*.refcache (git-LFS tracked).
cargo run -p grader --release -- --precompute corpus/

# Per candidate: grade wasm → per-testcase JSON + summary.json
cargo run -p grader --release -- candidate.wasm corpus/ results/<candidate>/

# Custom reference: any wasm implementing the ABI works. Default is the
# bundled Mesen2 build at reference/mesen.wasm.
cargo run -p grader --release -- --reference my-ref.wasm candidate.wasm corpus/ results/<candidate>/
```

## Scoring: three sections

The overall score is the weighted sum of three independent sections.
Default weights, configurable in [`corpus/grader.yaml`](corpus/grader.yaml):

| Section | Weight | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| **Gameplay Replays** | 60% | Real gameplay with button presses — end-to-end behavior under input |
| **Procedural Tests** | 20% | CPU, memory, timers, DMA — deterministic self-checking ROMs |
| **Audio**            | 20% | Per-frame log-mel spectral distance vs Mesen2 |

```
overall = 0.60 × replay + 0.20 × procedural + 0.20 × audio
```

## Building from source

The bundled `reference/mesen.wasm` is enough to grade. To rebuild it
from source (Mesen2 fork at `third_party/mesen`):

```bash
git submodule update --init --recursive
reference/build-mesen.sh wasm      # → reference/mesen.wasm
cargo build --workspace
```

input.description: Read assistant notes around regressions

content.content:
12:20 Still running. Quick procedural subset on the new build in parallel (memory allows two single-thread graders). 

12:23 Procedural: 10/16 pass. Looking at the remaining failures' screens. 

12:24 Now the lazy timer sync, start delay, and a halt fast-forward to the next PPU/timer event (halting games currently step 1 cycle at a time). 

12:25 Builds. Validating on the timer/VRAM tests. 

12:26 ppu-vram-mirror now passes. Checking the timer values. 

12:26 Reload test went 0/7 → 4/7, start-stop is off by one tick on the second case. To understand the remaining cases I'll read the test ROM's source (a hardware test, not emulator code). 

12:29 timer-start-stop now passes. The baseline is still going; checking which testcase it's on. 

12:29 Running the full replay set on the current build in the background while I investigate game divergences. 

12:29 Meanwhile, setting up the oracle frame-diff loop (dump Mesen2 frames and ours, find the first divergent frame). 

12:30 Frame 0 already differs completely, which suggests a boot-frame offset. Checking how the harness defines boot frames. 

12:41 We now raise IRQs slightly earlier than Mesen. Rather than guess the dot, I'll have the tracer run Mesen ahead on divergence and report the exact line/dot at which it enters the IRQ. 

12:43 That run is from an older build; stopping it and grading the current build on the full corpus. 

12:43 The copy never ran (pkill matched its own shell). Redoing it cleanly. 

12:43 Only my own probe matched; nothing is running. Launching the full v6 grade. 

12:44 While that runs (~28 min), checking that the native test suite still passes. 

12:46 All 8 regression tests pass. While the full grade runs, looking at the mgba-dma failure. 

12:46 Builds. Quick-checking DMA tests (the full v6 grade is still running alongside). 

12:48 1248/1256 now — 8 subtests left. Checking the suite's DMA test definitions to see what those could be. 

12:48 8 of 1256 DMA subtests remain (likely SRAM/word-width corner cases); the test is pass/fail, so I'll leave it documented. Checking the full v6 grade progress. 

12:48 Only procedural results so far. Meanwhile I'll compare DirectSound game audio directly: adding WAV output to the native runner and dumping goodboy from both emulators. 

12:49 Audio is grossly misaligned in places (we're playing where Mesen is silent and vice versa). First checking how the harness treats audio during boot frames, since the reference dump is 0.1 s longer. 

12:49 The grader drains boot audio on both sides (the oracle's dump doesn't, hence the extra 0.1 s). Checking goodboy video sync first, since audio can't match if gameplay diverges. 

12:50 Nearly every frame differs by a colour effect: our background shows a blended green circle and different brightness. Comparing exact pixel values. 

12:50 Pixels match at frame 50 but during fades ours is consistently one step behind, which suggests a one-frame phase lag. Testing frame-shift matches. 

12:50 No single frame shift explains it, so the fade arithmetic itself may differ. Checking the PPU's brightness/alpha formulas. 

12:54 DMA cost now matches to within 2 cycles over a 40k-cycle transfer. Next divergence: right after the DMA we take an IRQ that Mesen doesn't take until 27 instructions later. Looking at the context. 

12:55 Close, but one IRQ in each game is still taken an instruction early. Making the tracer print context at each mismatch to identify which IRQ source. 

12:55 The VBlank line rose *exactly* on an instruction boundary; Mesen counts that as rising during the next instruction. The latency check must be strict (`<`). 

12:57 Wrong sentinel: forcing `prev_step_start = 0` makes the check *fail*; it needs to be MAX to make the IRQ immediately eligible. 

12:57 Now we enter the IRQ directly on wake like Mesen. Letting the tracer advance Mesen to the vector in this case so the drift tells me the exact exit delay. 

12:59 The halt delay moved the first divergence earlier (a different halt path). Inspecting it. 

13:00 Mesen spends a few non-advancing execs waking up; generalizing the tracer to let a stalled Mesen catch up before comparing. 

13:09 The lag isn't the same on goodboy (~1248 samples) as on tonc-snd1 (~512). Measuring it over time windows to see whether it's constant per game or drifting. 

13:11 While that grades, running the lockstep tracer across the remaining games to find their first divergences. 

13:12 Every game now runs 230k–490k instructions in exact lockstep before its first divergence. Investigating each, starting with celeste (Mesen takes an IRQ we don't). 

13:47 v10's scores are identical to v8's to four decimals on almost every test, which is suspicious given how much timing changed. Verifying which wasm was actually graded. 

13:47 Different binaries, yet identical scores. Checking whether per-frame data differs at all. 

13:47 The first key press is at frame 69 and divergence starts at frame 70, so our input latency differs from Mesen's. Checking direction: does our frame 70 match Mesen's 69 or 71? 

13:48 **Huge effect:** goodboy now differs from Mesen in only **48 of 900 frames** (previously ~840). Making sure `reset` also clears the latched keys, then re-checking a couple of other games. 

13:49 Launching the full grade on this build (v11: key latching + prefetch fixes + I/O read fixes). 

13:49 While v11 grades: chip-advance differs from frame 1 (a 3-line tear). Looking at the diff mask to see whether this is our whole-scanline rendering at HBlank vs Mesen's progressive rendering. 

14:02 Both piugba and chip-advance produce ~2× the samples at a reported rate of 32768, confirming the 65536 Hz mode. Implementing SOUNDBIAS-selected sample rate and resolution. 

14:03 Removing the now-unused import, then quick-grading the affected audio cases plus controls. 

14:06 piugba audio jumps **0.06 → 0.70**; controls unchanged. chip-advance stays low because its gameplay itself diverges (video 0.10). Looking at a later chip-advance frame. 

14:06 Our frame shows corrupted tile graphics (top-right) where Mesen shows the level (top-left) — a content bug, not just timing. Finding where it starts (range 33–52). 

14:07 Mesen shows a **mosaic** fade (pixelated logo); we render it un-mosaiced — the PPU doesn't implement MOSAIC at all. Looking at the BG/OBJ render paths to add it. 

14:07 Mosaic needs to change the *sampling* coordinates per layer (layers share one line buffer). Reading the text and affine BG samplers to patch them. 

14:07 Implementing BG mosaic (text, affine, bitmap) and OBJ mosaic for regular sprites, plus the bitmap-mode OBJ tile restriction. 

14:08 Builds. Checking chip-advance against the oracle again. 

14:08 Mosaic fixed the fade ranges (33–52, 122–141). The playfield corruption remains; looking at where it first appears (frame 143). 

14:08 Frame 143 looks visually identical but nearly every pixel differs slightly — likely colour-effect rounding. Checking actual pixel values. 

14:09 Our darken effect is consistently one step brighter: we compute `I − ⌊I·EVY/16⌋`, Mesen computes `⌊I·(16−EVY)/16⌋`. Switching to the reference's rounding. 

14:09 Fade range 143–176 now matches. Next: 182–209 and the playfield from 270. 

14:09 The title-screen scroller text should be clipped to a band (window), but ours draws it over the whole screen. Dumping the PPU registers at that frame. 

14:10 No windows are used; mode 1 with alpha blending. The difference could be per-scanline raster effects. Checking which rows differ at frame 182 to see if it's a raster boundary. 

14:10 Rows 84+ show our affine BG2 with diagonal stripes where Mesen shows a clean background, so affine parameters/reference points differ. Dumping BG2's affine registers. 

14:11 While it grades, assembling the `results/` folder (summaries + per-test tables for each run) and documenting the input-latch and sample-rate findings. 

14:11 Updating the README's deliverables table to point at the real result files and new docs/tools.
